# Illisajātaka (Ja 78)

**ID:** Ja 78
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Illisajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Two Illisas
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja78
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Illisajātaka* (Ja 78) is a story in the Ekanipāta of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877; Macdonald, Mandala and Landscape]. Translated into English by Bhikkhu Sujato under the title *The Two Illisas*, the core canonical verse (*ubho khañjā...*) describes two seemingly indistinguishable men who are both lame, bow-legged, squinting, and bearing a wart, baffling onlookers as to which of them is the true Illīsa [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921b; Fausböll 1877].

The narrative framework is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the story concerning a miserly treasurer named Maccharikosiya from the town of Sakkharā near Rājagaha, who possessed eighty crores yet refused to share or consume his wealth [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the introductory story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha sends the Elder Moggallāna to subdue the miser and transport him, his wife, and their cakes to Jetavana; there, the cakes multiply inexhaustibly to feed the monastic assembly—a food miracle compared by modern scholars to Islamic and biblical motifs [Glasenapp 1966; Sujato 2011; Burlingame 1921a]. To explain that Moggallāna had subdued the miser before, the Buddha narrates the past story: the miser had been Illīsa, Moggallāna was Sakka (the king of the gods), Ānanda was the king, and the Bodhisatta was the barber (*kappaka*) [Burlingame 1921a; Fausböll 1877]. Notably, this is identified as the only instance in the Jātaka collection where Maudgalyāyana appears without Śāriputra, taking the form of Sakka [Powers 2009].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports automated or curated cross-canonical parallels for Ja 78 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, secondary studies note that the figure of Illīsa corresponds to the householder Hilliśāla in the Sanskrit *Karmavibhaṅga* and related narratives preserved in the Chinese Buddhist canon [Kudo 2004]. Within Pali commentarial literature, the introductory tale is virtually identical word-for-word with the story of Macchariya-Kosiya in the commentary to *Dhammapada* verse 49 [Burlingame 1921a, 1921b].
